title: Right to Information and Administrative Transparency

content.overview: The right to information is a statutory and constitutional dimension of administrative transparency. The Right to Information Act, 2005 creates enforceable access to information held by public authorities, subject to defined exemptions. Transparency supports accountability and informed participation in governance.
content.glance: Identify the public authority and the information sought; test whether an exemption applies; apply the public-interest override where relevant; and follow the statutory request and appeal route.
content.study: Transparency is both a governance value and a legal regime. The RTI Act obliges public authorities to disclose information on request and proactively, subject to exemptions such as national security, personal privacy and fiduciary confidentiality. The public-interest override may require disclosure even of exempt information in appropriate cases. Appeals lie to departmental appellate authorities and Information Commissions. Constitutional free-speech values inform interpretation but the Act remains the primary statutory framework. Current-law framing: ground the analysis in the RTI Act and the Constitution. Do not treat BSA 2023 as the source of RTI doctrine.

sections.heading: Transparency as a Governance Value
sections.body: Openness in administration supports accountability, reduces arbitrariness and enables citizen participation.

sections.heading: RTI Act Framework
sections.body: The Act defines public authorities, the right to information, exemptions and the institutional machinery of Information Commissions.

sections.heading: Exemptions and Public Interest
sections.body: Exemptions are specific and must be construed carefully. Public interest may justify disclosure of otherwise exempt material.

sections.heading: Procedure and Appeals
sections.body: Requests, fees, timelines, first appeals and second appeals to Information Commissions structure enforcement.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.body: RTI is not a substitute for discovery in pending litigation or a tool to harass; exemptions and process limits apply.

provisions.title: Freedom of speech and expression (informational dimension)

examples.title: Ordinary information request
examples.body: A citizen seeks copies of policy guidelines held by a public authority. Unless an exemption applies, disclosure follows the Act.

examples.title: Personal information claim
examples.body: A request seeks personal information of a public servant. Exemption analysis under the Act is fact-specific; official information is not automatically personal.

hypotheticals.question: Must every document of a public authority be disclosed?
hypotheticals.analysis: No. Exemptions under the Act protect specified interests.

hypotheticals.question: Is personal information of public servants always exempt?
hypotheticals.analysis: Exemption analysis is fact-specific; official information is not automatically personal.

distinctions.title: RTI disclosure vs discovery in litigation
distinctions.left: Statutory information-access regime against public authorities
distinctions.right: Procedural discovery between parties in a pending case

questionsAndAnswers.question: How should an RTI problem be analysed?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: I. Identify public authority and information. II. Test exemptions. III. Apply public-interest override if relevant. IV. Follow statutory appeal route.

questionsAndAnswers.question: What should submissions contain?
questionsAndAnswers.answer: Public authority status; information sought; exemption analysis; public interest; precise disclosure or appellate relief.
